location: I-V, 13.306; ex Count Severino. Part of legacy of Count Severino, 1566, also consisting of “a regal, a harpsichord, six viols, five cornetts, and one lira.”¹
pitch: B-natural, somewhat flat, with Schnitzer mouthpiece.
dimensions: bo 10.8, be 94, le 2646, slide sec. entry 11, slide sec. exit 10.5, slide sec. 1611, bell sec. 1052, overlap 17, bell sec. entry 12.5.
remarks: Reconstructed from nine original fragments, mostly tuning bits, crooks, slide-bows, bell-bows.²   No signature on garland. Rim wire has elaborate leaf pattern. One flat bell stay, narrow, in “column” shape, with hinge and pin, eyelet on bell pipe side. Ferrules have leaf pattern, as on bell garland. Flat slide stays, almost identical to 1560ca. Slide tubes are new work; slide works well. Slide bow has ring with saddle. Repair 455mm from end of bell. Ring in bell bow with saddle. Ferrules in slide and bell sections match. Ferrules have crown pattern at one end, leaf pattern, like garland, in middle, tendril pattern, like rim wire, on rings. Examined by the author, March 2001.
footnotes: According to Van der Meer & Weber 1982:72. Paganuzzi (1987:28) thinks that the instrument identified as 1560ca is the one referred to in the legacy; Van der Meer & Weber think that the simplicity of the instrument, and the insciprtion "FILARMONIA," argue against this theory. They speculate that an instrument included as part of a legacy would more likely be an expensive one, and point to fragments of an obviously expensive trombone existing in I-V (see Van der Meer & Weber 1982: 129).

The fragments shown in the photo in Van der Meer & Weber 1982: 129 appear to this writer to derive from two trombones, a hypothesis that is in fact supported by Paganuzzi (1987:27-28); one of the fragments may in fact be from instrument #1560ca. Interestingly, one of the fragments is a “pigtail”-shaped tube more commonly seen on trumpets than trombones. The fragments are not clearly described in the text, and are not given separate catalogue numbers.
